challenges.title: Bikes bring the revenue. Do they bring the profit?

brief.subject: Where does our profit come from?
body: Bikes are most of what we sell, so I plan the buying budget around them. Before next year's plan I want to see each product category on two measures: revenue and profit.
Use every order line in the data. Profit for a line is the line total minus quantity times the product's standard cost.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which category earns the profit, how the margins compare, and what it means for the budget.
facts: Revenue is LineTotal in ADW_Sales_orders_detail (one row per order line, after discounts).
StandardCost sits on ADW_Dim_Product. The category name is two joins away, through the subcategory table.

questions: Which category brings in the most revenue?
What margin does each category earn?
Does the ranking change when you rank by profit instead of revenue?

frame.nudge: Revenue and profit can rank the categories in a different order. What would you need to know about each line besides what it sold for?
tree: Where does profit come from?
Revenue by category
Cost by category (quantity × standard cost)
Margin = profit ÷ revenue, and each category's share of total profit
hyp: Bikes lead on revenue and on profit.
A small category may earn a much higher margin than bikes.
traps: Cost is per unit, so multiply by OrderQty before you subtract.
Divide profit by revenue for the margin. Do not average the margins of single lines.
Product to category takes two joins (product, subcategory, category). Miss one and the rows multiply or vanish.

tables: One row per order line with quantity and line total.
Standard cost and the subcategory of each product.
Links a product to its category.
Order header; the detail table already has line totals.
Regions are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders_detail: one row per order line. Every other table here is a lookup with one row per key, so the joins do not multiply rows.
Chain: detail → product → subcategory → category.
data.goal: One row per category: revenue, profit and margin %. Then add each category's share of total revenue and total profit.
data.skeleton:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName AS category
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                         -- profit: line total minus quantity x standard cost
     , ...                         -- margin %
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p ON ____
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON ____
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc ON ____
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
data.solution:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName                                   AS category
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)                   AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost) / 1000000.0, 2) AS profit_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost) / SUM(d.LineTotal), 1) AS margin_pct
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p             ON p.ProductID = d.ProductID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON sc.ProductSubcategoryID = p.ProductSubcategoryID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc    ON pc.ProductCategoryID = sc.ProductCategoryID
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: Subtracting the unit cost without multiplying by quantity understates cost on every multi-unit line.
Standard cost here is the current value on the product table. The cost history table would give a more exact answer.

extra_sql.title: Share of revenue vs share of profit (SUM ... OVER () turns each total into a share; feeds the chart)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT pc.ProductCategoryName AS category
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal) / SUM(SUM(d.LineTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost)
             / SUM(SUM(d.LineTotal - d.OrderQty * p.StandardCost)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_profit
FROM ADW_Sales_orders_detail d
JOIN ADW_Dim_Product p             ON p.ProductID = d.ProductID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductSubCategory sc ON sc.ProductSubcategoryID = p.ProductSubcategoryID
JOIN ADW_Dim_ProductCategory pc    ON pc.ProductCategoryID = sc.ProductCategoryID
GROUP BY pc.ProductCategoryName
ORDER BY pct_of_revenue DESC

metrics: Sum of line total minus quantity × standard cost.

viz_specs.title: Accessories punch above their weight on profit
viz_specs.sub: Share of total revenue and total profit by category, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two shares per category on one scale: grouped bars. The gap between the two bars is the story.

model: Bikes earn the profit: $7.9M of $9.4M in total (85%), on $94.7M of revenue.

Their margin is thin at 8.4%, though. Accessories earn 50% on only 1.2% of revenue, so they make 6.8% of profit. Components are the weak spot: $11.8M of revenue, a 4.2% margin and only $0.49M of profit, less than accessories.
Keep the buying budget on bikes, and look at pricing and cost on components. Check one thing before acting: standard cost is today's value, so the margins would shift a little with the cost history.
checks: I joined all four tables and multiplied cost by quantity.
I compared revenue rank with profit rank.
I used margin and share of profit, not revenue alone.
I named one caveat about cost.

challenges.title: Which sales territory grew fastest in 2013?

brief.subject: Territory growth, 2013 vs 2012
body: I'm splitting next year's sales targets by territory and I want to start from what grew last year. Please compare 2013 with 2012 for each of the ten territories.
Use revenue (SubTotal) and compare full years only.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: who grew fastest, how you measured it, and which territory needs attention.
facts: ADW_Sales_orders has a TerritoryID on each order. Names live in ADW_Dim_Territory.

questions: Which territory grew fastest in percent?
Which territory added the most dollars?
Did any territory shrink?

frame.nudge: A territory that doubled from a tiny base and a territory that added the most dollars are not always the same one. Which of the two matters for setting targets?
tree: Who grew in 2013?
Revenue per territory in 2012 and in 2013
Growth in percent and in dollars
Which territories sit below zero
hyp: The fastest growers are outside the US.
The biggest percent gain comes from a small starting base.
traps: Filter to the two full years. 2011 and 2014 are partial and would distort the comparison.
Percent growth hides the starting size. Put the dollar gain next to it.
Use >= and < on dates instead of BETWEEN with an end date.

tables: One row per order with date, territory and subtotal.
Line level; the order header already has the subtotal.
Products are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order, so SUM(SubTotal) per territory is safe.
ADW_Dim_Territory: one row per territory, so the join keeps one row per order.
data.goal: One row per territory: revenue in 2012, revenue in 2013, dollar gain and growth %, best first.
data.skeleton:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT t.TerritoryName
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2012 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2012_m
         , ...                                  -- the same for 2013
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
    JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t ON ____
    WHERE ____                                 -- the two full years
    GROUP BY t.TerritoryName
)
SELECT TerritoryName, rev_2012_m, rev_2013_m
     , ...                                      -- gain in $M
     , ...                                      -- growth %
FROM yearly
data.solution:
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT t.TerritoryName
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2012 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2012_m
         , SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2013 THEN o.SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0 AS rev_2013_m
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders o
    JOIN ADW_Dim_Territory t ON t.TerritoryID = o.TerritoryID
    WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2012-01-01' AND o.OrderDate < '2014-01-01'
    GROUP BY t.TerritoryName
)
SELECT TerritoryName
     , ROUND(rev_2012_m, 2)                                 AS rev_2012_m
     , ROUND(rev_2013_m, 2)                                 AS rev_2013_m
     , ROUND(rev_2013_m - rev_2012_m, 2)                    AS gain_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * (rev_2013_m - rev_2012_m) / rev_2012_m, 0) AS growth_pct
FROM yearly
ORDER BY growth_pct DESC
watch: The CASE WHEN pivot puts both years on one row, so growth is a plain subtraction.
Without the date filter, the 2011 and 2014 orders are summed into no column but still cost you time to explain.

metrics: Sum of SubTotal per territory and year.

viz_specs.title: Europe and Australia grew fastest, two US territories shrank
viz_specs.sub: Revenue growth 2013 vs 2012 by territory.
viz_specs.why: One value per category, ranked: bars from a zero line, so shrinking territories point down.

viz_specs.title: In dollars the gains are close
viz_specs.sub: Revenue added in 2013 vs 2012, $M.
viz_specs.why: The same ranking in dollars shows which gains are big and which come from a small base.

model: Germany grew fastest in percent (+366%), followed by France (+144%), the United Kingdom (+130%) and Australia (+99%).
Germany started from $0.55M, so its gain of $2.02M is similar to the other three. In dollars France added the most (+$2.25M). Northeast (-9%) and Southeast (-19%) shrank, and Central was flat.

Set the Europe and Australia targets from their dollar gains instead of their percentages, and ask the Northeast and Southeast teams what changed. One caveat: this is two years, and fast growth in a small market does not carry forward by itself.
checks: I compared full years only.
I looked at percent and dollars together.
I named the territories that shrank.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Online has most of the orders. Who brings the money?

brief.subject: Is online the main channel yet?
body: The dashboard shows far more online orders than sales-rep orders, and the online team wants more budget. Before I answer, I want to see both channels on orders and on revenue.
Please also show how the split changed from year to year.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which channel brings the revenue, why order counts mislead, and what to do about the budget.
facts: OnlineOrderFlag in ADW_Sales_orders: 1 = online, 0 = sales rep.
One row per order. Revenue = SubTotal.

questions: What share of orders is online, and what share of revenue?
How large is the average order in each channel?
Is the split changing from year to year?

frame.nudge: If one channel has 90% of the orders, does it have 90% of the revenue? What number links the two?
tree: Which channel matters?
Orders and revenue per channel
Average order value per channel
The same split by year
hyp: Online wins on order count but sales reps win on revenue.
Online's share of revenue is growing.
traps: A flag of 0 and 1 is unreadable in a report: label it with CASE WHEN.
Compare shares of the whole, not raw counts.
2011 starts in May and 2014 ends in June, so judge the yearly trend by shares, not by totals.

tables: Everything is on the order header: flag, date and subtotal.
Line level; not needed for channel totals.
Territories are not part of this question.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order. COUNT(*) is orders, SUM(SubTotal) is revenue.
No join is needed. The whole answer comes from one table.
data.goal: One row per channel: orders, % of orders, revenue, % of revenue, average order value.
data.skeleton:
SELECT CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE ____ END AS channel
     , COUNT(*) AS orders
     , ...                      -- % of all orders: use SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER ()
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                      -- % of all revenue
     , ...                      -- average order value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE ____ END
data.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END AS channel
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)          AS pct_of_orders
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)                         AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(SubTotal) / SUM(SUM(SubTotal)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0)                          AS avg_order_value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 'Online' ELSE 'Sales rep' END
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: The GROUP BY must repeat the CASE expression, not the alias, in SQL Server.
SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () is the grand total of the grouped counts. It does not need a second query.

extra_sql.title: The same split by year
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS online_m
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS sales_rep_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END) / SUM(SubTotal), 0) AS online_pct_of_revenue
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year

viz_specs.title: Online is 88% of the orders and 27% of the revenue
viz_specs.sub: Share of orders and revenue by channel, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two shares per channel: grouped bars. The flip between the two bars is the whole message.

viz_specs.title: Sales reps lead in every year
viz_specs.sub: Revenue by channel and year, $M. 2011 starts in May and 2014 stops in June.
viz_specs.why: Two groups across four years: grouped bars, same colour per channel.

model: Sales reps bring the revenue: they write 12% of the orders but 73% of the revenue.

An average sales-rep order is worth $21,148, against $1,061 online, so 20 online orders equal one rep order. Online's share of revenue fell to 19% in 2012, then rose to 25% in 2013 and 42% in the first half of 2014, but sales reps led every year.

Do not move the budget on order counts. Keep the rep channel funded and ask the online team how they plan to raise the basket size. The data does not say whether the two channels serve the same kind of customer, so the comparison is a first look.
checks: I compared share of orders with share of revenue.
I used average order value to explain the gap.
I looked at the trend by year.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue grew in 2013: more customers or bigger orders?

brief.subject: What drove 2013, and is 2014 a decline?
body: Revenue in 2013 was about 30% above 2012, yet the average order looks smaller. I need to know where the growth came from: more customers, customers ordering more often, or bigger orders.
The dashboard also shows 2014 falling off a cliff. I present to the board next week and I don't want to explain a collapse that isn't real.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: the main driver, why order value fell, and what to say about 2014.
facts: Revenue is SubTotal in ADW_Sales_orders (before tax and freight).
That table has one row per order.

questions: Which of customers, orders per customer and order value moved most between 2012 and 2013?
Why did the average order value fall?
Is the 2014 drop real?

frame.nudge: Revenue is a product of simpler pieces. Which pieces can you measure, and can they move in opposite directions?
tree: What drove 2013 revenue?
Revenue = customers × orders per customer × average order value
Which piece moved most from 2012 to 2013
Whether each year in the data is complete
hyp: The customer count grew a lot.
Order value fell because the mix shifted toward smaller online orders.
traps: Check the date range before comparing years. A part-year looks like a decline.
Divide each total by the right count: customers for orders per customer, orders for order value.
An average can fall because the mix of orders changed, even if no single order got smaller.

tables: One row per order with date, customer, channel flag and value.
Line level; order totals already sit on the header.
Not needed for a company-wide view.
grain: ADW_Sales_orders: one row per order, so COUNT(*) is orders and COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) is customers.
OnlineOrderFlag: 1 = online, 0 = sales rep.
data.goal: One row per year: orders, customers, orders per customer, average order value, revenue. Check the date range first.
data.skeleton:
-- Step 0: is every year complete?
SELECT MIN(OrderDate), MAX(OrderDate) FROM ADW_Sales_orders;

-- Step 1: the drivers by year
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , COUNT(*) AS orders
     , COUNT(DISTINCT ____) AS customers
     , ...        -- orders per customer
     , ...        -- average order value
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
data.solution:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate)                                   AS order_year
     , COUNT(*)                                         AS orders
     , COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID)                       AS customers
     , ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID), 3) AS orders_per_customer
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*), 0)               AS aov
     , ROUND(SUM(SubTotal) / 1000000.0, 2)              AS revenue_m
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year

pre.title: Step 0: date range
pre.sql: SELECT MIN(OrderDate) AS first_order, MAX(OrderDate) AS last_order FROM ADW_Sales_orders

watch: Orders per customer divides orders by distinct customers, not by rows.
2011 starts in May and 2014 ends in June. Compare full years only (2012 against 2013).

extra_sql.title: Index of 2013 vs 2012 (feeds the chart)
extra_sql.sql:
WITH y AS (
    SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
         , COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID)                  AS customers
         , 1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS orders_per_customer
         , SUM(SubTotal) / COUNT(*)                    AS aov
         , SUM(SubTotal)                               AS revenue
    FROM ADW_Sales_orders
    GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
)
SELECT 'Customers' AS driver, ROUND(100.0 * b.customers / a.customers, 0) AS index_2012_100
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Orders per customer', ROUND(100.0 * b.orders_per_customer / a.orders_per_customer, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Average order value', ROUND(100.0 * b.aov / a.aov, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Revenue', ROUND(100.0 * b.revenue / a.revenue, 0)
FROM y a JOIN y b ON a.order_year = 2012 AND b.order_year = 2013

metrics: Distinct customers with at least one order in the year.
2013 value ÷ 2012 value × 100. Revenue is the product of the three drivers.

viz_specs.title: Customers drove the growth and order value fell
viz_specs.why: Four ratios against one baseline: bars with a reference line at 100.

dig.title: Why did order value fall? Split by channel
dig.sql:
SELECT YEAR(OrderDate) AS order_year
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS online_share_of_orders_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS aov_online
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN SubTotal ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN OnlineOrderFlag = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS aov_sales_rep
FROM ADW_Sales_orders
GROUP BY YEAR(OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year
dig.read: In 2013 online orders average about $853 and sales-rep orders about $20,582. Online went from 70% of orders in 2012 to 89% in 2013, so the average fell with the mix.

model: Customers drove the growth: in 2013 there were 3.5 times as many as in 2012, while the average order value fell to 36% of its 2012 level.
Revenue rose from $33.5M to $43.6M. Orders per customer barely moved (103% of 2012). Online orders, which are small (about $853), went from 70% to 89% of all orders and pulled the average down.

2014 is not a collapse. The data stops on 30 June 2014, so that year holds six months. Compare January to June 2014 with January to June 2013 before it goes to the board. This shows what changed, not why more customers arrived.
checks: I split revenue into customers × frequency × order value.
I checked the date range before comparing years.
I explained the lower average with mix.
I said what to do about 2014.

challenges.title: Is the Central office really the weakest at closing deals?

brief.subject: Central says it is not the problem. Is it?
body: Three regional offices (Central, East and West) sell the same product line. At the last review a manager said Central closes fewer deals than the others and asked to move pipeline to East and West.
Before I move any accounts I need to know whether the gap in win rate is real. Count closed deals only: Won or Lost. Open deals have no outcome yet.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: is there a gap, how sure are you, and what should Sofia do.
facts: Win rate = Won ÷ (Won + Lost).
Each sales agent belongs to one regional office, in CRM_sales_teams.

questions: What is each office's win rate on closed deals?
How many deals sit behind each rate?
Is the gap bigger than the normal wobble of a rate?

frame.nudge: A small gap between three rates only matters if it is bigger than the wobble you would expect by chance. What do you need besides the rates themselves?
tree: Is Central weaker?
Win rate per office on closed deals
Number of deals behind each rate
The size of the gap against the margin of error
hyp: Central's rate is the lowest, but only by a little.
A gap this small could be noise.
traps: Open deals (Prospecting, Engaging) are not outcomes. Leave them out.
A rate from a small group moves more than a rate from a large one, so read the deal counts.
A ranking of three close numbers is a weak basis for moving pipeline.

tables: One row per deal with its stage.
Maps each agent to a regional office.
Customer companies; not part of this question.
Product list; not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal. Filter to Won and Lost.
CRM_sales_teams: one row per agent, so the JOIN does not duplicate deals.
data.goal: One row per regional office: closed deals, won deals and win rate.
data.skeleton:
SELECT t.regional_office
     , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = ____ THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS won
     , ...                          -- win rate %
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage IN (____)
GROUP BY t.regional_office
data.solution:
SELECT t.regional_office
     , COUNT(*)                                                       AS closed_deals
     , SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)          AS won
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS win_rate_pct
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
WHERE p.deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY t.regional_office
ORDER BY win_rate_pct
watch: Leaving open deals in the denominator pulls every office's rate down by a different amount.
After the WHERE, COUNT(*) counts closed deals only. Check that it equals Won + Lost.

metrics: Closed deals per office. It sets how far a rate can move by chance.
Best office rate − worst office rate, in percentage points.
About 2 × √(rate × (1 − rate) ÷ deals). If two whiskers overlap, the gap may be chance.

viz_specs.title: Three offices, one overlapping band
viz_specs.sub: Win rate on closed deals, with the margin of error as whiskers.
viz_specs.why: Points with whiskers need no zero baseline. Overlapping whiskers say the gap may be chance.

model: No. The three offices win at almost the same rate, so there is no case for moving pipeline away from Central.
On 6,711 closed deals the win rates are Central 62.6%, East 63.0%, West 63.9%. Best and worst differ by 1.4 points, and each rate can move by about 2 points by chance, so the whiskers overlap.
Leave the allocation as it is and look for the real driver in another cut, such as product or sector. This says the offices do not differ, not that the win rate is good.
checks: I answered yes or no first.
I used closed deals only.
I compared the gap with the margin of error.
I did not invent a story for a small gap.

challenges.title: Which manager leads on revenue, and is it the team or one agent?

brief.subject: Bonus review: revenue by manager
body: I'm preparing the manager bonus review. I have a ranking of the six managers by revenue and I want to check it before I use it.
Count won deals only, with close_value as revenue. Show me the managers, and the best agents behind them.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: who leads, what sits behind the lead, and whether the ranking is fair for a bonus.
facts: Each agent reports to one manager, in CRM_sales_teams.
Revenue = close_value of deals with deal_stage = 'Won'.

questions: Which manager's team brings in the most revenue?
Who are the top agents, and how much of the total does each bring?
Is the manager ranking driven by the team or by one person?

frame.nudge: A manager's total is the sum of their agents. If one agent is much bigger than the rest, what does the manager ranking really measure?
tree: Is the manager ranking fair?
Revenue and won deals per manager
Revenue per agent, to compare teams of different size
The top agents and their share of the total
hyp: The top manager has one star agent.
Without that agent the ranking looks different.
traps: Count Won deals only. Lost and open deals have no revenue.
Divide by the number of agents who actually closed deals, not by the team list.
Rank agents with RANK() OVER, since TOP is not portable.

tables: One row per deal with the agent, stage and value.
Agent to manager and regional office.
Customers are not part of this question.
Products are not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal, filtered to Won.
CRM_sales_teams: one row per agent, so the join does not duplicate deals.
data.goal: One row per manager: agents, won deals, revenue and revenue per agent. Then list the top five agents with their share of total revenue.
data.skeleton:
SELECT t.manager, t.regional_office
     , COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent) AS agents
     , COUNT(*) AS won_deals
     , ...                          -- revenue in $M
     , ...                          -- revenue per agent
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage = ____
GROUP BY t.manager, t.regional_office
data.solution:
SELECT t.manager
     , t.regional_office
     , COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent)                               AS agents
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)                    AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / COUNT(DISTINCT t.sales_agent), 0) AS revenue_per_agent
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY t.manager, t.regional_office
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: COUNT(*) here counts won deals because the WHERE keeps only Won rows.
The teams table lists 35 agents, but only 30 closed deals. Counting from the pipeline gives the real team size.

extra_sql.title: Top five agents (RANK() OVER plus a share of the total; feeds the second chart)
extra_sql.sql:
WITH agent AS (
    SELECT p.sales_agent, t.manager
         , COUNT(*)           AS won_deals
         , SUM(p.close_value) AS revenue
    FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
    JOIN CRM_sales_teams t ON t.sales_agent = p.sales_agent
    WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
    GROUP BY p.sales_agent, t.manager
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *
         , RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC)                 AS rnk
         , ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1)    AS pct_of_total
    FROM agent
)
SELECT rnk, sales_agent, manager, won_deals
     , ROUND(revenue / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , pct_of_total
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY rnk

metrics: Manager revenue ÷ agents who closed at least one deal.
Agent revenue ÷ revenue of all agents.

viz_specs.title: Melvin Marxen's team leads on revenue
viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by manager, $M.
viz_specs.why: One value per manager, ranked: bars from zero.

viz_specs.title: One agent closes more than twice the next
viz_specs.sub: Top five agents by won revenue, $M.
viz_specs.why: The same ranking one level down shows how far the first agent stands from the rest.

model: Melvin Marxen's team leads with $2.25M, but the lead rests on one agent.
Darcel Schlecht closed $1.15M, 12% of all revenue and 2.4 times the next agent. Without Darcel, Melvin's team would have $1.10M, level with Dustin Brinkmann's $1.09M.

Do not use the manager ranking alone for the bonus. Show revenue per agent and the share of the top agent next to it. One caveat: this is a single year, and one strong year from one agent says little about the manager.

I looked below the manager level.
I quoted the share of the top agent.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue by product series: why does the join lose a product?

brief.subject: Revenue by product series
body: I want won revenue for each product series (GTX, MG and GTK) for the roadmap meeting. The series name is in the products table, and the deals are in the pipeline table.
A colleague already ran a join and sent me the numbers, but the total looks too low compared with the sales report. Please redo it and tell me what went wrong.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: revenue by series, why the first total was low, and what to fix.
facts: Won revenue = close_value of deals with deal_stage = 'Won'.
Series live in CRM_products (columns product, series, sales_price).

questions: How much won revenue does each series bring?
Does the revenue by series add up to the total of all won deals?
If not, which product is missing and why?

frame.nudge: After a join, compare the total with the total before it. If the two differ, which rows did the join drop?
tree: Why is the total too low?
Total won revenue before the join
Total won revenue after the join
Which product names fail to match
hyp: One product name is spelled differently in the two tables.
The missing product is a big seller.
traps: An INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows without a warning. Always check the total.
Look for the unmatched value with a LEFT JOIN and IS NULL.
Fix the name in the query with REPLACE, or on the data side if you own the table.

tables: Deals with product, stage and value.
Agents are not part of this question.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal.
CRM_products: one row per product, so the join keeps one row per deal as long as the names match.
data.goal: Won revenue by series that adds up to the full total.
data.skeleton:
-- Step 1: which names fail to match?
SELECT p.product, COUNT(*) FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
LEFT JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = p.product
WHERE pr.product IS ____
GROUP BY p.product;

-- Step 2: join again with the name fixed
SELECT pr.series, SUM(p.close_value) AS revenue
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = REPLACE(p.product, ____, ____)
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY pr.series
data.solution:
SELECT pr.series
     , COUNT(*)                                                    AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)                    AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(p.close_value) / SUM(SUM(p.close_value)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_revenue
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = REPLACE(p.product, 'GTXPro', 'GTX Pro')
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY pr.series
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC

pre.title: The first attempt: a plain join on the product name
pre.sql:
SELECT pr.series
     , COUNT(*)                                  AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(p.close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)  AS revenue_m
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = p.product
WHERE p.deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY pr.series
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC

watch: The plain join returns a believable table. Only the total shows that revenue is missing.
The unmatched check also matches open and lost deals, so the count is higher than the won deals alone.

dig.title: Which name fails to match?
dig.sql:
SELECT p.product, COUNT(*) AS deals
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
LEFT JOIN CRM_products pr ON pr.product = p.product
WHERE pr.product IS NULL
GROUP BY p.product
dig.read: The pipeline writes one product as GTXPro, the products table writes GTX Pro. Those deals fall out of the plain join.

extra_sql.title: Won revenue by product (shows which product was lost)

SELECT product
     , COUNT(*)                                  AS won_deals
     , ROUND(SUM(close_value) / 1000000.0, 2)    AS revenue_m
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline
WHERE deal_stage = 'Won'
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC

metrics: Total after the join − total before the join. It should be zero.

viz_specs.title: GTX brings almost three quarters of the revenue
viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by product series, $M.
viz_specs.why: Three categories with one value each: bars from zero.

viz_specs.title: The product that fell out of the join is the top seller
viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by product, $M. The highlighted bar is GTXPro.
viz_specs.why: Seven products ranked by revenue: bars show how big the missing piece is.

model: The GTX series brings $7.3M (73% of the $10.0M won), MG brings $2.3M (23%) and GTK $0.4M (4%).

The first total was low at $6.5M because the pipeline spells one product GTXPro and the products table spells it GTX Pro. The join dropped 729 won deals worth $3.5M, which makes it the top-selling product.

Use the fixed query for the roadmap and ask whoever owns the pipeline to correct the spelling at the source. One caveat: GTK 500 has only 15 won deals, so its share moves a lot with a single big sale.
checks: I compared the total before and after the join.
I found the unmatched product with a LEFT JOIN.
I fixed the name instead of dropping the rows.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which customer sector is worth targeting?

brief.subject: Which sector should the next campaign target?
body: We have budget for one sector-focused campaign. I'd like to pick the sector where we win the most revenue, and I'd like to know whether that comes from closing better or from having more deals.
Use closed deals (Won or Lost) and the account's sector.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which sector brings the most revenue, whether it closes better than the others, and what to target.
facts: The sector of each customer is on CRM_Accounts, linked by the account name.
The data spells one sector technolgy. Keep the spelling when you filter.

questions: Which sector brings the most won revenue?
Does any sector have a clearly higher win rate?
Is a sector's revenue driven by deal count or by deal size?

frame.nudge: Revenue in a sector is deals × win rate × deal size. Which of the three actually differs between sectors?
tree: Which sector to target?
Revenue per sector
Win rate per sector
Deals and average deal size per sector
hyp: Win rates are similar, so revenue follows the number of deals.
A small sector may have a high average deal size.
traps: Use closed deals for the win rate, and Won deals for revenue and deal size.
Open deals have no account in many rows, so the inner join drops them. Closed deals all have one.
Do not read a 1 or 2 point gap in win rate as a strength.

tables: Deals with account, stage and value.
Agents are not part of this question.
Products are not part of this question.
grain: CRM_sales_pipeline: one row per deal.
CRM_Accounts: one row per account, so the join does not duplicate deals.
data.goal: One row per sector: closed deals, win rate, won revenue and average won deal size.
data.skeleton:
SELECT a.sector
     , COUNT(*) AS closed_deals
     , ...                          -- win rate %
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                          -- average won deal size
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_Accounts a ON ____
WHERE p.deal_stage IN (____)
GROUP BY a.sector
data.solution:
SELECT a.sector
     , COUNT(*)                                                                  AS closed_deals
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS win_rate_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN p.close_value ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN p.deal_stage = 'Won' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0)         AS avg_won_deal
FROM CRM_sales_pipeline p
JOIN CRM_Accounts a ON a.account = p.account
WHERE p.deal_stage IN ('Won', 'Lost')
GROUP BY a.sector
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: Average deal size divides revenue by won deals, not by closed deals.
Lost deals have a close_value of 0, so summing them in does no harm, but dividing by them does.

viz_specs.title: Retail leads on won revenue
viz_specs.sub: Won revenue by customer sector, $M.
viz_specs.why: Ten sectors ranked by one value: bars from zero.

viz_specs.title: Win rates barely differ between sectors
viz_specs.sub: Win rate on closed deals by sector.
viz_specs.why: On a 0 to 100 scale, near-equal bars make the point: the sector does not change how well we close.

model: Retail brings the most won revenue ($1.87M), but it does not close better than the other sectors.
Win rates sit between 61% and 65% across all 10 sectors, so revenue follows the number of deals. Retail has 1,267 closed deals, the most of any sector, and an average won deal of $2,337.

Target retail if the aim is volume. If the aim is a better close rate, no sector offers it, so look at product or agent instead. The data covers one year and 6,711 closed deals, so keep the campaign small and measure it.
checks: I used closed deals for the win rate and won deals for revenue.
I separated volume from win rate.
I did not read a small gap as a strength.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which product categories earn the most profit?

brief.subject: Category profit for the range review
body: We review the product range twice a year and the last review used revenue only. This time I want profit as well, so we don't drop or push a category for the wrong reason.
Use all orders in the data. Revenue is quantity times the unit price in USD, and profit is quantity times (unit price − unit cost).
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which categories earn the profit, whether margins differ, and what that means for the review.
facts: GBE_Sales has one row per order line with the product key and the quantity.
Prices and costs are in USD on GBE_Products, which also holds the category.

questions: Which categories bring the most revenue and the most profit?
Do the margins differ much between categories?
What are the five most profitable subcategories?

frame.nudge: Revenue and profit can rank categories differently. What would make that happen, and how would you check it?
tree: Which categories earn the profit?
Revenue and profit per category
Margin = profit ÷ revenue per category
Whether the profit ranking differs from the revenue ranking
hyp: Computers lead on both.
Margins are close across categories, so the two rankings match.
traps: Price and cost live on the product, quantity lives on the sale. Multiply them line by line before you sum.
Do not average the margin of single products. Divide total profit by total revenue.
Do not sum Unit_Price_USD alone: a line of 3 units earns 3 times the price.

tables: Order lines with product key and quantity.
Category, unit price and unit cost in USD.
Stores are not part of this question.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line. Quantity is on this row.
GBE_Products: one row per product, so the join keeps one row per order line.
data.goal: One row per category: revenue, profit and margin %. Then list the five most profitable subcategories.
data.skeleton:
SELECT p.Category
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , ...                         -- profit in $M: quantity x (price - cost)
     , ...                         -- margin %
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON ____
GROUP BY p.Category
data.solution:
SELECT p.Category
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2)                          AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD)) / 1000000.0, 2)      AS profit_m
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD))
             / SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD), 1)                                   AS margin_pct
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY p.Category
ORDER BY revenue_m DESC
watch: The margin is profit divided by revenue at the category level, not an average of product margins.
Round only in the final SELECT. Rounding inside the sum changes the totals.

extra_sql.title: Top five subcategories by profit
extra_sql.sql:
WITH sub AS (
    SELECT p.Subcategory
         , SUM(s.Quantity * (p.Unit_Price_USD - p.Unit_Cost_USD)) AS profit
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    GROUP BY p.Subcategory
), ranked AS (
    SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY profit DESC) AS rnk
    FROM sub
)
SELECT rnk, Subcategory, ROUND(profit / 1000000.0, 2) AS profit_m
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 5
ORDER BY rnk

metrics: Sum of quantity × (unit price − unit cost).

viz_specs.title: Computers and home appliances lead on revenue and profit
viz_specs.sub: Revenue and profit by category, $M, all years.
viz_specs.why: Two values per category in the same unit: grouped bars.

viz_specs.title: Margins are close in every category
viz_specs.sub: Profit as a percent of revenue, by category.
viz_specs.why: On a 0 to 100 scale, near-equal bars show that margin does not separate the categories.

model: Computers earn the most profit ($11.3M on $19.3M of revenue), followed by home appliances ($6.3M). Together they make 54% of all profit.

Margins are almost the same everywhere, from 55% (Games and Toys) to 61% (Music, Movies and Audio Books), so the profit ranking follows the revenue ranking. The most profitable subcategory is Desktops ($5.63M).

Judge the range by volume, since no category is a profit trap and none is a hidden winner. Games and toys are the smallest at $0.72M of revenue. This uses list prices and costs, so it ignores discounts and returns.
checks: I multiplied quantity by price and cost on each line.
I compared revenue rank with profit rank.
I computed margin from totals.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which country's stores earn the most per square meter?

brief.from_: Marcus Hale, Head of Retail Operations
brief.subject: Store space: where does it work hardest?
body: We are choosing where to put the next store budget. Total revenue by country favors the big markets, so I want revenue per square meter of store space.
Use 2019, the last full year before the drop in 2020. Count physical stores only (the online store has no floor space), and only stores that were open for the whole year.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: which countries use their space best, which worst, and what to do with the budget.
facts: GBE_Stores has the country, the floor space (Square_Meters) and the open date of each store.
Online orders sit under StoreKey = 0. Exclude them.

questions: What is the revenue per square meter in each country?
Which stores should be left out so the comparison is fair?
How big is the gap between the best and the worst country?

frame.nudge: Revenue per square meter divides two things that live in different tables. At what level do you add each one up so that neither is counted twice?
tree: Which countries use space best?
Revenue per store in 2019
Floor space per store
Both rolled up to country, then revenue ÷ space
hyp: The country with the most stores is not the one with the best revenue per square meter.
Small stores earn more per square meter.
traps: Add revenue up per store first. Joining sales to stores row by row repeats the floor space on every sale.
Stores that opened in 2019 had only part of a year. Leave them out.
Some stores sold nothing in 2019. They are not in the revenue table and drop out of the join.

tables: Order lines with the store key and the date.
Unit price to turn quantity into revenue.
Country, floor space and open date.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line, many per store. Sum to one row per store before you join to the stores table.
GBE_Stores: one row per store, so each store's floor space is counted once.
data.goal: One row per country: stores, floor space, 2019 revenue and revenue per square meter.
data.skeleton:
WITH store_rev AS (
    SELECT s.StoreKey, SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.StoreKey <> 0
      AND s.Order_Date >= ____ AND s.Order_Date < ____
    GROUP BY s.StoreKey
)
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*) AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters) AS square_meters
     , ...                       -- revenue per square meter
FROM GBE_Stores st
JOIN store_rev r ON ____
WHERE st.Open_Date < ____
GROUP BY st.Country
data.solution:
WITH store_rev AS (
    SELECT s.StoreKey
         , SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) AS revenue
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.StoreKey <> 0
      AND s.Order_Date >= '2019-01-01' AND s.Order_Date < '2020-01-01'
    GROUP BY s.StoreKey
)
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters)                             AS square_meters
     , ROUND(SUM(r.revenue) / 1000000.0, 2)              AS revenue_m
     , ROUND(SUM(r.revenue) / SUM(st.Square_Meters), 0)  AS usd_per_sqm
FROM GBE_Stores st
JOIN store_rev r ON r.StoreKey = st.StoreKey
WHERE st.Open_Date < '2019-01-01'
GROUP BY st.Country
ORDER BY usd_per_sqm DESC
watch: Joining sales rows straight to stores and then summing Square_Meters adds each store's space once per sale.
Revenue and floor space must cover the same stores, so both come from the joined rows.

extra_sql.title: For comparison: all stores per country, whether or not they sold in 2019
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT st.Country
     , COUNT(*)                                       AS stores
     , SUM(st.Square_Meters)                          AS square_meters
FROM GBE_Stores st
WHERE st.StoreKey <> 0
GROUP BY st.Country
ORDER BY st.Country

metrics: Sum of quantity × unit price per store in 2019.
Country revenue ÷ country floor space, same stores in both.
Open before the year starts and with sales in the year.

viz_specs.title: US stores earn more than twice what Australian stores do per square meter
viz_specs.sub: 2019 revenue per square meter of floor space, USD, stores open all year.
viz_specs.why: One value per country, ranked: bars from zero.

model: The United States uses its space best at $242 per square meter in 2019, and Australia uses it worst at $104.

The gap is 2.3 times. Canada ($234) is close behind the US, then Italy ($181) and France ($164), while Germany ($125) and the Netherlands ($105) sit near the bottom. The US result comes from 20 comparable stores, so it is not one lucky shop.
Put the next budget into the US and look at Australia and the Netherlands before adding space there. Floor space is only one driver: store age, local prices and product mix are not in this data.
checks: I summed revenue per store before joining to the stores table.
I used comparable stores only.
I excluded the online store.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Revenue fell in 2020. Did online hold up better than stores?

brief.subject: 2020 against 2019, by channel
body: Revenue dropped sharply in 2020. The board asks whether our online store cushioned the fall, because the plan for next year leans on it.
Compare each quarter of 2020 with the same quarter of 2019, for online and for stores separately.
brief.ask: Reply in three sentences: how big the fall was, whether online did better, and what that means for the plan.
facts: Online orders have StoreKey = 0 in GBE_Sales. All other keys are physical stores.
Revenue = quantity × unit price (USD).

questions: How much did total revenue fall in 2020?
In which quarters did the fall happen, for online and for stores?
Did online fall less than the stores?

frame.nudge: Compare each 2020 quarter with the same quarter in 2019, not with the quarter before it. Why does that matter for retail data?
tree: Did online cushion the fall?
Revenue per year, to size the fall and check the date range
2020 as a percent of 2019 for each quarter and channel
Online's share of revenue in each year
hyp: Online fell less than stores in the first months of the crisis.
The fall is large in both channels in the second half.
traps: Check the date range first. The last year in the data is a part-year.
Compare the same quarter of two years to remove seasonality.
Do not put 0 and 1 flags on a chart. Say online and stores.

tables: Order lines with date, store key and quantity.
Unit price to turn quantity into revenue.
Online is already identified by StoreKey = 0.
Customers are not part of this question.
grain: GBE_Sales: one row per order line.
GBE_Products: one row per product, so the join does not duplicate lines.
data.goal: One row per quarter: 2020 revenue as a percent of the same quarter in 2019, for online and for stores.
data.skeleton:
-- Step 0: size the year and check the dates
SELECT YEAR(s.Order_Date), ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2), MIN(s.Order_Date), MAX(s.Order_Date)
FROM GBE_Sales s JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY YEAR(s.Order_Date);

-- Step 1: one row per quarter, four sums (online/store x 2019/2020)
WITH q AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1' ... END AS quarter
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN ____ ELSE 0 END) AS online_2019
         , ...
    FROM ...
)
SELECT quarter, ...        -- 2020 as % of 2019 for each channel
FROM q
data.solution:
WITH q AS (
    SELECT CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 6 THEN 'Q2'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 9 THEN 'Q3'
              ELSE 'Q4' END AS quarter
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS online_2019
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey = 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2020 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS online_2020
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey <> 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2019 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS store_2019
         , SUM(CASE WHEN s.StoreKey <> 0 AND YEAR(s.Order_Date) = 2020 THEN s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD ELSE 0 END) AS store_2020
    FROM GBE_Sales s
    JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
    WHERE s.Order_Date >= '2019-01-01' AND s.Order_Date < '2021-01-01'
    GROUP BY CASE WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 3 THEN 'Q1'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 6 THEN 'Q2'
              WHEN MONTH(s.Order_Date) <= 9 THEN 'Q3'
              ELSE 'Q4' END
)
SELECT quarter
     , ROUND(100.0 * online_2020 / online_2019, 0) AS online_pct_of_2019
     , ROUND(100.0 * store_2020 / store_2019, 0)   AS store_pct_of_2019
     , ROUND((online_2020 + store_2020) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_2020_m
     , ROUND((online_2019 + store_2019) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_2019_m
FROM q
ORDER BY quarter

pre.title: Step 0: revenue per year and the date range
pre.sql:
SELECT YEAR(s.Order_Date) AS order_year
     , ROUND(SUM(s.Quantity * p.Unit_Price_USD) / 1000000.0, 2) AS revenue_m
     , MIN(s.Order_Date) AS first_day
     , MAX(s.Order_Date) AS last_day
FROM GBE_Sales s
JOIN GBE_Products p ON p.ProductKey = s.ProductKey
GROUP BY YEAR(s.Order_Date)
ORDER BY order_year

watch: T-SQL has no QUARTER() function. A CASE on MONTH() works in every dialect.
A pivot with CASE WHEN keeps both years on one row, so the percent is a plain division.

metrics: Revenue in a 2020 quarter ÷ revenue in the same 2019 quarter × 100.
Online revenue ÷ total revenue in the year.

viz_specs.title: Both channels fall away after the first quarter
viz_specs.sub: 2020 revenue as a percent of the same quarter in 2019.
viz_specs.why: Two channels across four quarters: two lines on the same scale.

model: Revenue fell 49% in 2020, from $18.3M to $9.3M, and online did not cushion it for long.
Q1 was level with 2019 in both channels. In Q2 online held up better (69% of 2019 against 56% for stores), but by Q3 online was at 30% and stores at 29%, and in Q4 at 22% and 20%.
Do not build next year's plan on online alone: it fell nearly as far as the stores. The data shows what dropped, not why, so ask Operations whether stock, delivery or demand caused it.
checks: I compared the same quarter across two years.
I split online from stores.
I checked the date range.
I gave one action and one caveat.

challenges.title: Which device should get the extra search budget?

brief.subject: +30% on Google non-brand search: where should it go?
body: We sell plush toys online. Nearly all paid traffic comes from Google non-brand search, and Finance approved 30% more budget there.

Our agency quotes about $2.50 per click, the same on desktop and mobile. Treat one click as one website session. Use the last 6 months (19 Sep 2014 to 18 Mar 2015): the site changed a lot before that.
Is the extra budget worth it, and on which device? I have five minutes on Friday.
brief.ask: Deliver a three-sentence answer: the call, the evidence, the action.
facts: Channel: utm_source = 'gsearch' and utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'.
The $2.50 click price comes from Maya, not from the database.

questions: What does one click earn after product cost and refunds?
Is that the same on desktop and mobile?
Is the gap real or noise?

frame.nudge: Every click costs money and earns money. What do we earn per click after product cost and refunds, and is that the same for every kind of visitor?
tree: Is more budget worth it?
Earn per session vs $2.50 paid per session
Does earn-per-session differ by device?
Is any gap real or noise, and stable over months?
hyp: Desktop earns more per session than mobile.
Mobile sits below break-even at $2.50, desktop above.
traps: Revenue is not profit: subtract cost of goods and refunds.
Sessions without an order earn $0 but still cost a click: divide by all sessions.
Three years of data mix very different sites: use the recent window.
Text 'NULL' in UTM columns means direct/organic traffic.

tables: Every click is a session; holds channel, campaign and device.
Price and cost per order, linked to the session.
Profit is not revenue: refunds must come off.
Order-level price and cost already sit in orders.
Funnel data; not needed for click economics.
grain: website_sessions: one row per visit. Start here so non-buyers stay.
orders: at most one order per session. LEFT JOIN from sessions.
order_item_refunds: several rows per order for 8 orders. Pre-aggregate per order before joining.
data.goal: One row per device: sessions, orders, conversion rate, revenue and net margin per session.
data.skeleton:
WITH refunds AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT s.device_type
     , COUNT(*) AS sessions
     , COUNT(____) AS orders          -- which column is NULL when there is no order?
     , ...                            -- conversion rate %
     , ...                            -- net margin per session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON ____
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE ____                            -- channel and 6-month window
GROUP BY s.device_type
data.solution:
WITH refunds AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(refund_amount_usd) AS refund_usd
    FROM order_item_refunds
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT s.device_type
     , COUNT(*)                                          AS sessions
     , COUNT(o.order_id)                                 AS orders
     , ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(o.order_id) / COUNT(*), 2)    AS cvr_pct
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd) / COUNT(*), 3)             AS revenue_per_session
     , ROUND(SUM(o.price_usd - o.cogs_usd - COALESCE(r.refund_usd, 0)) / COUNT(*), 3) AS net_margin_per_session
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE s.utm_source = 'gsearch' AND s.utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'
  AND s.created_at >= '2014-09-19' AND s.created_at < '2015-03-19'
GROUP BY s.device_type
watch: INNER JOIN to orders drops every non-buyer, so conversion reads 100%.
Averaging only over buyers gives margin per order, not per click.
BETWEEN with an end date misses most of the last day on datetimes: use >= and <.

extra_sql.title: Month by month, desktop vs mobile (pivot with conditional aggregation, feeds the line chart)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(s.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(s.created_at) AS yr_month
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'desktop' AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'desktop' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS desktop_cvr
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'mobile' AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN s.device_type = 'mobile' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS mobile_cvr
FROM website_sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.website_session_id = s.website_session_id
WHERE s.utm_source = 'gsearch' AND s.utm_campaign = 'nonbrand'
  AND s.created_at >= '2014-09-19' AND s.created_at < '2015-03-19'
GROUP BY YEAR(s.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(s.created_at)
ORDER BY yr_month

metrics: Equals net margin per session: pay less and the click makes money.

viz_specs.title: Desktop clears the $2.50 click price; mobile does not
viz_specs.sub: Net margin per session, 19 Sep 2014 to 18 Mar 2015. Whiskers: 95% CI.
viz_specs.why: Two values against a threshold: bars from zero plus a price line. Whiskers show uncertainty.

viz_specs.title: The gap shows up every month
viz_specs.sub: Conversion rate by month and device. First and last month are partial.
viz_specs.why: Change over time: lines, same colour per device in both charts.

stats.prompt: Desktop converts at 10.2%, mobile at 3.6%. Which approach shows the gap is not luck?
options: Paired t-test
Desktop and mobile are different visits, not pairs.
Two-proportion z-test plus a CI for the difference
Yes/no outcome per session in two independent groups; the CI gives the size of the gap.
Correlation of device and revenue
Device is a category; correlation does not give the gap in business terms.
No test, the chart is obvious
A decision needs an interval you can defend.
read: Desktop's whole interval sits above $2.50. Mobile's sits below. The verdict does not hinge on noise.
Margin intervals use a Welch (unequal variance) interval on session-level margin; with 25k+ sessions per group the normal approximation is fine.
watch: A tiny p-value does not say why. We compared groups; mobile ads may use other keywords or pages.
Most sessions earn $0, so check the interval, not just the mean.

model: Yes for desktop, no for mobile. At $2.50 a click desktop makes money and mobile loses it, so the extra budget should go to desktop only.

A desktop session earns $3.87 net margin (after cost of goods and refunds), a mobile session $1.36. That is $1.37 profit per desktop click and -$1.14 per mobile click. Desktop converts 10.2% of sessions against 3.6% on mobile (gap 6.6 points, 95% CI 6.3 to 6.9) and leads every month.

About 4,029 extra clicks a month on desktop is worth about $5,510 a month, against $2,375 if spread like today. Lower mobile bids below $1.26 a click or pause mobile. Caveat: click price usually rises with volume, so raise desktop bids in steps; we have not tested why mobile converts worse.
checks: My first sentence is the call (yes / no / where).
I used net margin per session over all sessions, not revenue.
I compared each device with the $2.50 click price.
I quoted an interval, and one caveat.

challenges.title: Refunds jumped this summer. Blip or trend, and which product?

brief.subject: Refund rate: is something broken?
body: Refund numbers looked ugly in the autumn review, and I cannot tell whether it is one product, one bad month or a new normal.
Please check May 2014 onward. Define the refund rate as items refunded ÷ items sold, grouped by the month the item was bought.
If something broke, I need to know which product and when, so I can chase the supplier.
brief.ask: Deliver three sentences: which product, how big and for how long, and what Dan should do.
facts: Window: items bought from 1 May 2014 to 19 Mar 2015.
Tables hold items sold (order_items), refunds and the product list.

questions: Which product has an unusual refund rate?
When did the spike start, and did it persist?
Is the spike bigger than the normal ups and downs?

frame.nudge: A rate has a top and a bottom. Which product, which month? Split the overall rate in two directions before you decide anything.
tree: Is the refund rate a problem?
Which product(s) have an unusual rate?
When did it start and does it persist? (month by month)
Is the spike bigger than normal ups and downs?
hyp: One product drives the spike.
The spike is limited to a few months and then returns to normal.
A product can have a high rate without a spike: check both views.
traps: Count refunded items against items sold, not against refund rows or orders.
Group by purchase month; refunds arrive later but belong to the sale.
Compare against the other products in the same months, not against a different period.
The product with the highest overall rate is not necessarily the one with the spike: look at the rate over time as well as the total.

tables: Items sold: product and purchase date.
Header level; items are the right grain for an item rate.
grain: order_items: one row per item sold. This is the denominator.
order_item_refunds: at most one row per refunded item (LEFT JOIN to keep non-refunded items).
products: join for names.
data.goal: Refund rate by product, then by month for the problem product vs all others.
data.skeleton:
SELECT p.product_name
     , COUNT(*) AS items_sold
     , SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN ____ ELSE 0 END) AS items_refunded
     , ...                              -- refund rate %
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN ____ r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= ____
GROUP BY p.product_name
data.solution:
SELECT p.product_name
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS items_sold
     , SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS items_refunded
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS refund_rate_pct
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN order_item_refunds r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= '2014-05-01'
GROUP BY p.product_name
ORDER BY refund_rate_pct DESC
watch: INNER JOIN to refunds keeps only refunded items, so the rate reads 100%.
COUNT(r.order_item_id) and the SUM(CASE...) give the same numerator; pick one and be consistent.
Dividing by orders instead of items changes the rate for multi-item orders.

extra_sql.title: Month-by-month (pivot with conditional aggregation)
extra_sql.sql:
SELECT YEAR(i.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(i.created_at) AS yr_month
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id = 1 AND r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS original_mr_fuzzy
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id <> 1 AND r.order_item_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / SUM(CASE WHEN i.product_id <> 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS other_products
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN order_item_refunds r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
WHERE i.created_at >= '2014-05-01'
GROUP BY YEAR(i.created_at) * 100 + MONTH(i.created_at)
ORDER BY yr_month

metrics: Items refunded ÷ items sold, by purchase month.
The rate in months without the spike, for the same product.
(Spike rate − baseline) × items sold in the spike months.

viz_specs.title: One product, two months
viz_specs.sub: Refund rate by purchase month, since May 2014.
viz_specs.why: Change over time for two groups: two lines. A table of 11 months would hide the shape.

stats.prompt: Original Mr. Fuzzy: 13.5% refunded in Aug-Sep 2014 vs 3.6% in the other months. Which approach?
options: Two-proportion z-test plus CI on the two periods
Two independent groups of items with a yes/no outcome.
Average the monthly rates and compare means
Months have different volumes; averaging rates ignores that.
Correlation of month number and refund rate
A spike then recovery is not a linear trend.
No test needed
Even a big gap deserves an interval before you chase a supplier.
read: The spike is far outside normal variation, so it is a real event, not noise.
Excess refunds in the two months: about 199 items.
watch: A significant spike says nothing about the cause: batch, supplier, shipping or a listing error.
Two months is a short run: confirm October stayed normal before calling it a blip.

model: It is a blip on one product. The Original Mr. Fuzzy had a refund spike in August and September 2014 and has been back to normal since October.

Its refund rate was 13.5% in those two months against 3.6% in other months (gap 9.9 pts, 95% CI 8.3 to 11.4). Other products stayed flat. Separately, The Birthday Sugar Panda has the highest rate over the whole window (5.8%) with no spike: a steady, higher baseline rather than an event.

No ongoing fix needed. Ask the supplier about Mr. Fuzzy items bought in Aug-Sep 2014 (about 199 extra refunds). Put a review of the Panda's steady rate on the list as a separate item. Caveat: the data does not show the cause; confirm with the refund reasons if Ops has them.
checks: I named the product and the months.
I compared the spike with the product's own baseline.
I said whether it persists.
I gave Dan one next step and one caveat.

challenges.title: The 2018 promotion: did it bring members who stay?

brief.subject: 2018 promotion: is it working?
body: In 2018 we ran a promotion that enrolled 971 members. The dashboard says 11.8% of them have cancelled against 12.4% of standard members, so I am told the promotion is as good as standard enrollment.
I want to repeat it next year. Is the comparison fair, and are promo members as loyal as standard ones?
brief.ask: Deliver three sentences: is the dashboard comparison right, what is the real picture, what should Ana do.
facts: Churn = member has a cancellation year.
Tables: ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History (one row per member).

questions: Is the dashboard comparing like with like?
What is the churn rate when both groups joined in the same year?
Is the gap bigger than chance?

frame.nudge: Who are the 'standard' members being compared against? When did they join, and for how long have they had the chance to cancel?
tree: Is the promotion as good as standard?
What does the dashboard compare, and is it like for like?
What is churn when both groups joined in the same year?
Is the difference bigger than chance?
hyp: Standard members include years of older enrollments with more time to cancel.
Compared within 2018, promo members cancel much more often.
traps: Members who enrolled in 2012 had six more years to cancel than members who enrolled in 2018.
Compare groups with the same exposure time: filter to the same enrollment year.
An overall average hides the cohort mix.

tables: Has enrollment type, enrollment year and cancellation year per member.
Flight behavior; not needed to measure churn.
Date dimension; years are already on the member row.
grain: ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History: one row per member.
Cancelled = Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL.
Enrollment_Type has two values: Standard and 2018 Promotion.
data.goal: Churn rate by enrollment type, first overall (the dashboard), then within the same enrollment year.
data.skeleton:
-- The dashboard view (all years)
SELECT Enrollment_Type
     , COUNT(*) AS members
     , SUM(CASE WHEN ____ IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
     , ...                    -- cancel rate %
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Type

-- The fair view: add Enrollment_Year to the GROUP BY
data.solution:
SELECT Enrollment_Year
     , Enrollment_Type
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS members
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_rate_pct
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Year, Enrollment_Type
ORDER BY Enrollment_Year, Enrollment_Type

pre.title: The dashboard view (all years)
pre.sql:
SELECT Enrollment_Type
     , COUNT(*)                                                         AS members
     , SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS cancelled
     , ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN Cancellation_Year IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS cancel_rate_pct
FROM ALT_Customer_Loyalty_History
GROUP BY Enrollment_Type

watch: The first query reproduces the dashboard: it is correct arithmetic and the wrong comparison.
Promo members exist only for 2018, so the like-for-like check is the 2018 row pair.

metrics: Members with a cancellation year ÷ members.
All members who enrolled in the same year.
Compare promo and standard within enrollment year 2018 only.

viz_specs.title: Fair comparison: promo members cancel five times as often
viz_specs.sub: Cancel rate by enrollment type. The 'All enrollees' bars are the dashboard comparison.
viz_specs.why: Two groups in two scopes: grouped bars. The jump between the scopes is the story.

stats.prompt: Promo vs standard members enrolled in 2018 (yes/no: cancelled). Which approach?
options: Two-proportion z-test plus CI on 2018 enrollees
Two independent groups with a yes/no outcome, same enrollment year.
Two-proportion z-test on all members
That repeats the unfair comparison with a p-value on top.
Paired t-test
Members are different people, not pairs.
Compare the means of CLV
CLV is a different question from cancellation.
read: Within 2018 the gap is large and the interval is far from 0.
Ratio: promo cancel rate is about 5.5x the standard rate in the same cohort.
watch: Promo members may differ in other ways (offer, channel, age). This is a comparison, not an experiment.
Cancellation is counted to date: both groups had the same exposure, so the comparison is fair, but the absolute rates will rise.

model: No. Promo members are much less loyal, and the dashboard hid it by comparing them with older standard members who had years longer to cancel.

Overall, 11.8% of promo and 12.4% of standard members cancelled. Within the 2018 cohort, where both groups had the same time, promo members cancelled at 11.8% vs 2.2% (gap 9.7 pts, 95% CI 7.6 to 11.8).

Do not repeat the promotion as designed. Test a version with a retention hook (for example a second-year benefit) and compare it with standard members from the same month. Caveat: promo members may differ in other ways; a randomized test would settle it.
checks: I explained why the dashboard comparison is unfair.
I compared groups within the same enrollment year.
I quoted the gap and its interval.
I proposed a next test.
